data.title: Oracle vs. Microsoft: One AI Hyperscaler Stock Is a Buy, the Other Is One to Watch, Says RBC
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) are both major players in the cloud computing market, with artificial intelligence now playing a central role in the growth story for both companies. Oracle has been gaining ground rapidly in cloud infrastructure, particularly as demand for AI computing power surges, while Microsoft’s Azure business continues to benefit from its huge enterprise customer base and deep investments in AI.

Back at the end of July, Microsoft delivered a strong set of quarterly results, highlighting continued momentum across Azure and its broader cloud business. Oracle has now followed with an impressive earnings report of its own, boosted by surging AI demand.

With both companies benefiting from the huge need for AI infrastructure and cloud services, the question for investors is which stock offers the more compelling opportunity right now.

Promotion

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

RBC analyst Rishi Jaluria, who covers both names, sees plenty to like in Oracle’s latest results. Revenue rose 30% year-over-year, cloud revenue jumped 62%, and EPS came in ahead of expectations. The standout was Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), where revenue surged 121% to $7.4 billion, accelerating sharply from the previous quarter. Total remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion, up 47%, helped by another $30 billion in AI cloud contracts.

Jaluria believes OCI’s momentum should continue as Oracle brings additional capacity online faster than expected. The company is also seeing strong demand for its infrastructure, with renewed GPU contracts carrying a 20% premium to previous agreements.

The outlook is similarly strong, with Oracle forecasting 30% to 34% revenue growth for the current quarter and 65% to 71% cloud growth, at the midpoint ahead of analyst expectations.

Looking at the big picture, Jaluria likes Oracle’s leadership in database software, its broad product portfolio and its position in enterprise resource planning. However, he remains cautious about the company’s acquisition history and “integration challenges,” as well as the intensely competitive cloud market. Longer sales cycles and geopolitical uncertainty also present risks, particularly as Oracle expands internationally.

“We remain watchful as the company navigates leaner margins and capital-intensive infrastructure buildout,” Jaluria summed up.

As such, Jaluria has a Sector Perform rating on ORCL shares, backed by a $165 price target (lowered from $190, implying the stock will deliver returns of 7% over the one-year time frame. (To watch Jaluria’s track record, click here)

Turning to Microsoft, Jaluria sees continued strength in Azure, with management forecasting around 44% to 45% constant-currency growth. Microsoft has changed how it reports its cloud businesses, with Azure now reported separately and Microsoft 365 Cloud bringing together commercial and consumer cloud businesses, along with GitHub Cloud and other developer cloud services and Security Copilot. Jaluria notes that Microsoft’s overall revenue, operating margin and EPS guidance remained unchanged despite the new reporting structure.

However, M365 Commercial Cloud growth was actually raised to 17% from 15%, while commercial seat growth is now expected to reach 7%, up from 6% in fiscal 2026.

“Stepping back, we see these changes improving visibility into key growth drivers,” the analyst said.

Accordingly, Jaluria rates MSFT stock as Outperform (i.e., Buy), while his $640 price target offers 12-month upside of 29.5%.

Unlike the RBC stance, the Street sees both names as Strong Buys. ORCL stock is expected to appreciate by 65% in the year ahead, given the average target stands at $254.32. Meanwhile, MSFT’s average target comes in at $571.41, a figure offering 12-month upside of 15%. (See ORCL stock forecast or MSFT stock forecast)

The best dividend stocks, of course, are those that pay the highest yield. If the yield is too low, it won’t beat inflation. But there’s no such thing as a dividend yield that’s ‘too high,’ so why settle for 4% when there are plenty of dividend payers offering yields of 7% or better?

data.title: No Game-Changer for Meta Stock, Says Oppenheimer
data.description:
Investors have reacted positively to the launch of Meta’s (NASDAQ:META) new AI agent, Muse, and its potential to boost the social media giant’s standing in the AI game.

Muse is designed to go beyond simply answering questions. The AI agent can carry out tasks on a user’s behalf, including managing emails and calendars, booking appointments, shopping online and working across different apps. For Meta, the launch represents another step toward turning its massive user base and heavy AI investment into something more significant than just a better chatbot.

However, Oppenheimer analyst Jason Helfstein is not convinced that Muse will deliver the boost the company is looking for.

Promotion

METQ: built for a short position on META

Helfstein sees several problems. First, he questions whether enough consumers will actually pay for the AI agent. He estimates Meta would need around 115 million paying subscribers to generate enough earnings upside to make a meaningful difference. At $20 a month, that would translate into roughly $27.5 billion in annual revenue, assuming an 80% incremental operating margin.

Competition is another issue. Consumers who are already prepared to pay for an AI agent may already have subscriptions to ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini, making it harder for Meta to persuade them to add another service.

But perhaps the biggest obstacle is trust. Helfstein argues that Muse will need access to users’ passwords to handle tasks such as e-commerce and other online services effectively. Yet Oppenheimer’s survey of 1,500 U.S. consumers suggests many people are not comfortable giving Meta that level of access.

Only 13% of respondents said they would share all their passwords with an AI agent, while 28% would consider doing so depending on the provider and 58% would refuse. Meta also ranked poorly on the question of which platforms consumers would trust with their passwords. Google scored 30%, Apple 23% and ChatGPT 16%, compared with just 8% for Meta.

Helfstein also points to relatively low consumer awareness of AI agents. While 41% of respondents had heard of them, they did not fully understand their capabilities, and only 10% had actually used one. Just 19% said they would pay for an agentic assistant, while 44% said they would not.

Finally, Helfstein sees a potential challenge from Apple. Google is expected to provide additional computing capacity for Apple Intelligence and Siri through Gemini, potentially giving Apple users a more capable AI assistant. With Apple and Google also enjoying greater consumer trust, Meta could have a tough time turning Muse into a major paid business.

To this end, Helfstein reiterated a Perform (i.e., Neutral) rating on the stock, without having a fixed price target in mind. (To watch Helfstein’s track record, click here)

Others on the Street do have targets and the average lands at $757.95, suggesting the stock will gain 16.5% in the months ahead. On the rating front, based on an additional 38 Buys and 6 Holds, the analyst consensus views this stock as a Strong Buy. (See META stock forecast)

data.title: ‘It’s an Outdated Trap,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) currently finds itself in an unusual position: record profits would normally be a warning sign for a memory stock, but this time they could be part of the bull case. The company is benefiting from an extraordinary shortage of memory chips as AI data centers consume supply faster than the industry can replace it. Micron’s latest results showed just how powerful the boom has become, with record revenue and profitability as demand continues to outstrip supply.

However, there is a catch. Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and history suggests that exceptionally high margins can eventually be followed by falling prices, weaker profits and a painful downturn.

That raises an important question for investors: is Micron approaching the top of another memory cycle, or is AI changing the cycle altogether?

Promotion

Discover why XOVR identified Kalshi as an attractive private investment opportunity.

Top investor Keithen Drury, who contributes to the Motley Fool and ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, believes investors shouldn’t assume that history will simply repeat itself.

The memory industry is cyclical largely because its products are commoditized. Micron competes with Samsung and SK hynix, and customers can move between suppliers when they can get a better price. That makes supply and demand critical to the industry’s profitability.

At the moment, though, demand is unlike anything Micron has seen before. Hyperscalers are spending huge sums on AI data centers, and those facilities require enormous amounts of memory. Demand has grown faster than Micron and its competitors can add production, creating a shortage that has pushed memory prices sharply higher. Micron itself says AI-driven demand is growing faster than the industry’s ability to increase supply.

That has translated into extraordinary margins. And this is where the historical argument becomes important. Over the past two decades, Micron’s profitability has moved dramatically with the memory cycle. The company experienced major downturns during the 2008-09 financial crisis and again in 2023. Even the previous major peak was followed by a substantial decline. Before reaching its current margin peak, Micron’s profitability previously peaked in fiscal Q4 2018, when gross margin reached 61% and operating margin hit 51.9%.

The obvious concern is that the current boom could eventually produce the same result. If new fabs bring enough capacity online, supply could catch up with demand. Memory prices could then fall, taking Micron’s margins and earnings with them.

Drury’s argument is that the timing could be very different this time.

Micron’s management expects the current supply tightness to persist beyond 2027, giving the company a longer period of unusually strong demand. And while additional capacity should eventually ease the shortage, that doesn’t necessarily mean the AI spending boom will end. The broader build-out of AI infrastructure is expected to continue for years, potentially keeping demand elevated even after the current supply crunch fades.

There is another important difference. Micron has signed multiyear strategic agreements with major customers that include committed volumes and pricing protections. The company says these contracts provide greater visibility and stability and could make its financial performance more predictable than in previous cycles.

That doesn’t mean Micron’s margins can stay at record levels forever. Drury expects profitability to normalize eventually. But if AI keeps demand strong through the end of the decade, Micron could remain highly profitable even after the current shortage ends. “I don’t think history will repeat itself for Micron’s stock through 2030, and that makes it a strong buy now,” the 5-star investor summed up. (To watch Drury’s track record, click here)

That is also the conclusion reached by the analyst consensus, a rating based on 30 Buys vs. 1 Hold. Shares are expected to gain 51% over the next year, given the average price target clocks in at $1,553.10. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: WDC, STX and SNDK: Which AI Storage Stock Is the Most Appealing Right Now? Top Investor Weighs In
data.description:
The AI revolution is driving a major expansion in data center capacity, and that is translating into unusually strong demand for storage.

Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC), Seagate Technology (NASDAQ:STX) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) are all seeing customers commit to storage capacity well in advance, giving the companies much better visibility into future demand than they typically have. But while all three are benefiting from the same trend, the deals they have secured offer different levels of protection, particularly when it comes to pricing.

Investor David Sparks, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, has compared the three stocks, focusing on how much future business is already secured and how much confidence investors can have in the earnings ahead.

Promotion

Double your STX exposure with Tradr's STXX

Western Digital has plenty of momentum. The company generated $3.75 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue, a 44% increase from a year earlier, while adjusted gross margin climbed to 54.4% and EPS more than doubled. Its customer base has also become heavily concentrated in the cloud, which accounted for 89% of revenue in the fiscal third quarter.

Sparks sees a potential weakness, however. Western Digital has secured major orders for 2026 and has longer-term arrangements with some of its biggest customers, but investors don’t have a clear picture of how much production is covered beyond the current year. If the storage market eventually turns lower, that could leave the company exposed when today’s agreements expire.

The valuation isn’t particularly demanding at around 14 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings. Sparks therefore sees enough to keep the stock interesting, but not enough contractual visibility to make it his preferred choice.

Seagate has given customers more certainty over both demand and pricing. The company says its build-to-order arrangements already establish the products customers will receive and the prices they will pay throughout calendar 2027. It has also allocated most of its nearline capacity, which is widely used by cloud data centers, through 2028.

The financial numbers are moving in the same direction. Seagate’s fiscal 2026 revenue increased 34% to $12.2 billion, while fourth-quarter revenue climbed 48% to $3.63 billion. Adjusted gross margin jumped to 52.7%, and adjusted EPS more than doubled to $5.71. Management expects first-quarter revenue of roughly $4.1 billion, implying growth of about 56% from a year earlier.

For Sparks, that combination matters because a significant portion of the expected growth is backed by customer commitments already in place. Seagate trades at around 15 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, putting it at a similar valuation to Western Digital.

Sandisk has taken a different approach to securing its future business. The company has agreements with eight customers covering a substantial portion of its upcoming production. More than half of its fiscal 2027 volumes and roughly two-thirds of fiscal 2028’s volumes are expected to fall under those contracts.

There is another important feature. The agreements include minimum pricing provisions, meaning Sandisk has some protection if memory prices weaken. Management says the contracts would represent at least $93.9 billion of revenue even at those contractual floor prices.

Sparks considers that a significant advantage, but there is still an unanswered question. Those pricing protections have yet to be put through a serious memory market downturn, so investors don’t know how they will perform when industry conditions become less favorable.

Sandisk is coming off an exceptional year, with fiscal 2026 revenue soaring 175% to $20.25 billion as memory prices rose and data center demand strengthened. That growth gives the company plenty of appeal, but Sparks remains cautious about assuming current conditions will last indefinitely.

So, down to business, which stock does Sparks think represents the best opportunity right now?

“My pick is Seagate. Its contracts already fix pricing for all of calendar 2027, and most of its nearline capacity is spoken for into the year after that. Growth is accelerating, too,” the 5-star analyst said.

As for the other two, Western Digital offers a similar valuation and is benefiting from the same strong demand environment. However, Sparks isn’t convinced that enough of its production is secured beyond 2026 to give him the same confidence as Seagate. Sandisk arguably has the most downside protection of the three thanks to its pricing floors, but those safeguards have yet to face a real industry downturn. Sparks would prefer to see how they hold up before taking a more bullish stance. (To watch Sparks’ track record, click here)

data.title: ‘Not Enough,’ Says Investor About Apple Stock
data.description:
Bucking Thursday’s trend, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) stock is in the green today after the tech giant unveiled one of its most significant new iPhone products in years: the $1,999 iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone.

The company also introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, with the lineup featuring upgraded cameras, the new A20 Pro chip and a range of Apple Intelligence improvements. The foldable is particularly important because it takes Apple into a smartphone category where rivals such as Samsung have already had several years to establish themselves. The event also marked the first major iPhone launch under new CEO John Ternus, giving investors an early look at how Apple plans to balance its famously cautious approach with the need to keep finding new sources of growth.

Apple has been benefiting from a strong iPhone cycle, while its Services business continues to provide a growing and highly profitable source of revenue. The iPhone remains the foundation of the ecosystem, but the company needs to keep finding ways to increase the amount customers spend on each device and deepen their engagement with its products and subscriptions. The foldable iPhone could help on both fronts, while Apple’s expanding AI capabilities could create another opportunity for Services. The question is whether these developments are enough to justify the premium valuation investors are currently paying for the stock.

For investor Kenio Fontes, the event lacked pizzazz and still reflected Apple’s cautious approach to innovation. While the iPhone Duo represents a major new product category, much of the iPhone 18 lineup looks familiar. Fontes sees that conservatism as understandable given the iPhone’s success, but believes Apple’s enormous cash flow gives it room to invest more aggressively in new products and features.

The iPhone Duo could nevertheless prove valuable. At $1,999, even modest adoption could lift Apple’s average selling price. Fontes uses a hypothetical scenario in which Apple sells roughly 77 million iPhones in a quarter, with 2% being Duo models. Under those assumptions, iPhone revenue could reach around $74.7 billion, compared with $54.2 billion in the most recent quarter.

The opportunity is not simply selling more expensive phones. The Duo could attract consumers who want a foldable but prefer Apple’s ecosystem, while encouraging existing customers to spend more across devices and services. Apple’s late entry could also fit its traditional strategy of allowing competitors to establish a market before entering with a more polished product. Strong foldable sales from Samsung and expectations for continued growth make that approach more credible.

Fontes also sees potential in Apple’s AI push. New Siri and other Apple Intelligence features could make newer devices more compelling and accelerate upgrade cycles. More importantly, some AI features have usage limits because they rely on powerful server models, potentially encouraging users to upgrade their iCloud+ subscriptions. With a large installed base already paying for cloud storage, higher AI limits could strengthen Services revenue.

Despite these positives, Fontes remains bearish on Apple stock because of its valuation. Even assuming 10% annual revenue growth through fiscal 2032 and gradual margin expansion, he estimates an annual total return of about 7.1%. Under more conservative, cyclical growth assumptions, that falls closer to 6.3%. In other words, Fontes believes Apple’s expected return is not high enough to compensate investors for the risks. With the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield around 4.9% and the S&P 500’s historical return around 10%, Fontes believes Apple does not currently offer a sufficient margin of safety. The company remains an exceptional business, but he believes too much of that quality is already reflected in the share price.

Accordingly, Fontes rates the stock a Sell. (To watch Fontes’ track record, click here)

data.title: 2 ‘Strong Buy’ Stocks Where the Bears Could Get Burned
data.description:
There’s been a long-term bullish trend in the markets, but that hasn’t stopped short interest in stocks. It may seem counterintuitive to sell short in a positive market, but short sellers can reap solid gains based on short-term volatility – if they are willing to shoulder higher risks.

And short selling involves risks. It’s basically a bet, no matter whether markets are going up or down, that a given stock will drop in the short term. Short sellers borrow shares, sell them, and then buy them back – and if the price has dropped in the meantime, the short seller realizes the difference as a profit.

The risk, of course, is that the stock might gain, and that’s a real concern for short sellers in today’s market.

data.title: ‘Stay Focused,’ Says Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
After the huge growth seen over the past year, Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) is now approaching a critical test. The challenge will be sustaining that growth without leading to the supply imbalances that have historically weighed on the NAND industry.

Demand remains strong, pricing has improved sharply, and the company has secured substantial long-term commitments from customers. The question now is whether Sandisk can maintain that favorable balance between supply and demand as the market expands. Its August investor day reinforced that strategy, with new agreements covering roughly half of FY2027 bits and two-thirds of FY2028 bits, alongside a long-term financial model targeting mid-to-high-teens revenue growth and roughly 80% gross margins.

Investor Andres Veurink believes the answer to that question is yes. He argues that Sandisk’s position is becoming more compelling precisely because the company is taking a disciplined approach to capacity. In his view, the tighter supply dynamics in NAND give Sandisk an edge over DRAM manufacturers and could work in its favor over the next several years.

The distinction comes down to supply. Veurink has been cautious on DRAM because improvements in manufacturing technology allow producers to squeeze substantially more bits from each wafer, while physical wafer capacity is also expanding. If both continue at a rapid pace, DRAM supply could eventually run ahead of demand, putting pressure on prices.

NAND works differently. Manufacturers can choose how quickly those productivity gains translate into additional supply. Sandisk has said output per wafer can grow by around 27% a year, but management has also made clear that it does not intend to introduce every new technology node simply because it is available. The aim is to increase production when the market actually needs it rather than risk another supply glut.

That discipline is central to Veurink’s thesis. Sandisk’s new business model agreements also provide another layer of protection, with committed volumes, minimum financial guarantees and structured pricing. The company says eight customers now account for about 50% of FY2027 bits and roughly two-thirds of FY2028 bits under these agreements.

The biggest threat, in Veurink’s view, is Chinese competitor Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC), which is rapidly expanding its NAND production. More capacity from YMTC could eventually put pressure on prices, but Veurink believes NAND’s overall supply outlook remains much healthier than DRAM’s.

He also sees an intriguing wildcard in Sandisk’s High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) technology. HBF is designed to bring much higher memory capacity to AI systems while addressing power and system-level constraints. Sandisk says the technology is gaining momentum as AI inference workloads expand.

“When modeled, even in a worst-case scenario, SNDK still looks fairly valued,” Veurink summed up. “That is the sort of investment I’m looking for, so I frankly don’t care much if the price has surged astronomically the last year, the fundamentals are still in place and that is all that matters.”

data.title: Micron vs. SK hynix: One AI Memory Stock Is Good, the Other Is Better, Says Investor
data.description:
The memory industry has become one of the biggest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence buildout. AI data centers require enormous amounts of high-speed memory and storage, while the long lead times and huge costs involved in expanding production have kept supply tight. That has driven memory prices sharply higher and created a powerful earnings cycle for companies such as Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY).

The key question for investors, however, is how sustainable this cycle is and which company is better positioned as AI workloads evolve. Investor Ignacio Planas Gonzalez focuses on the differences in their exposure to high-bandwidth memory (HBM), conventional DRAM and the emerging high-bandwidth flash (HBF) market.

Both companies are benefiting from surging memory prices and constrained supply. Micron has also secured strategic customer agreements covering roughly 20% of its DRAM production and about one-third of its NAND output. These contracts provide greater visibility into future demand and include substantial customer deposits, giving the company some protection from the extreme volatility that has historically characterized the memory industry.

Micron also has a strong balance sheet, with substantial net cash and record free cash flow. The investor notes that the stock trades at roughly 6.6 times forward earnings, which appears inexpensive. However, Planas Gonzalez cautions that traditional valuation measures can be misleading for cyclical companies. Memory stocks often trade at their lowest P/E multiples when earnings are close to their peak, meaning an apparently cheap stock can actually be reflecting unusually strong temporary profits.

SK hynix has a different advantage in HBM. Planas Gonzalez highlights the company’s roughly 50% share of the HBM market, compared with about 18% for Micron. SK hynix also has approximately 25% of the overall DRAM market. The investor points out that the company has already begun mass production and shipments of HBM4, the latest generation designed for Nvidia’s next-generation Rubin platform.

HBM is particularly important for AI training because GPUs need enormous amounts of bandwidth to process data. But Planas Gonzalez sees another potentially important opportunity in HBF. Rather than stacking DRAM like HBM, HBF stacks NAND and is designed to provide AI accelerators with substantially more memory capacity at a much lower cost per bit.

The investor believes this could become ever more important as AI moves from training toward inference and agentic applications. Larger models, longer context windows, intermediate outputs and greater concurrency could all increase the amount of data that needs to remain readily available. In Planas Gonzalez’s view, this creates a potentially significant new market for high-capacity memory.

SK hynix is working with Sandisk to develop and standardize HBF, with commercial availability expected in 2027. The investor sees this as an important differentiator because packaging and qualifying NAND specifically for AI workloads could make the product less commoditized and allow SK hynix to capture more value. Micron currently has no comparable HBF exposure.

There are still significant risks. Planas Gonzalez notes that memory remains highly cyclical, meaning a reversal in pricing could quickly damage earnings. Chinese manufacturer CXMT is also expanding aggressively and could put additional pressure on DRAM prices. SK hynix carries additional Korean market, currency and ADS-related risks.

Despite those concerns, the investor believes the current AI-driven cycle has enough structural support to continue. Supply is unlikely to catch up meaningfully before 2028, while the evolution toward inference and agentic AI could create new memory requirements.

That leaves Planas Gonzalez with a favorable view of both stocks, but a stronger preference for SK hynix. The investor rates Micron a Buy because of its financial strength, customer contracts and exposure to the memory upcycle. data.title: ‘Avoid Complications,’ Says Top Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) has emerged as one of the more striking growth stories in the memory market, with revenue and cash flow surging as demand for data storage has risen alongside AI infrastructure. Yet despite the rapid growth, the stock trades at roughly 10 times forward free cash flow, based on an estimate of around $24 billion in fiscal 2027 free cash flow.

The stock, then, is relatively inexpensive, although the biggest question for investors is whether today’s momentum can continue as year-over-year comparisons become more demanding.

It’s the combination of rapid growth and a seemingly modest valuation that makes Sandisk particularly interesting to top investor Michael Wiggins De Oliveira. His view is straightforward: the risks are real, but they are sufficiently obvious that much of them are already reflected in the share price. That leaves what he sees as considerable upside if the company can sustain even a portion of its current momentum.

Promotion

SNDK has a long & short ETF? Explore SNXX & SNDQ

De Oliveira argues that investors should resist the temptation to construct overly complicated investment theses. Instead, the focus should be on identifying a simple underlying trend and assessing whether the valuation adequately reflects it. In Sandisk’s case, the central argument is that the explosion in data generated by AI and neocloud companies is creating substantial demand for memory and storage. As companies accumulate enormous amounts of data, they need reliable and increasingly cost-effective ways to store it.

The investor expects Sandisk’s revenue to grow by roughly 140% year-over-year in fiscal 2027 (which started in July). Growth will inevitably slow as the company moves into the second half of the year and faces tougher comparisons, while weaker-than-expected NAND pricing could add pressure. However, De Oliveira believes investors do not need to predict precisely how much growth will slow because the current valuation already provides considerable room for error.

Sandisk’s financial position is another important part of the thesis. The company has no debt, while cash represents roughly 2% of its market cap, excluding long-term investments. Management has also committed to returning 100% of excess free cash flow to shareholders, potentially equivalent to around 5% of the company’s market value over the next year.

Most importantly, De Oliveira expects Sandisk to generate around $24 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2027. With the stock trading at roughly 10 times that estimate, he believes the market is placing a relatively low value on a business capable of producing enormous amounts of cash.

The main threat is NAND pricing, which can fluctuate sharply as supply and demand change. Sandisk’s exposure to shorter-term contracts adds another layer of uncertainty, although the company says it has secured four-year average contracts.

For De Oliveira, the investment thesis ultimately comes down to valuation and cash generation. If Sandisk looks unlikely to produce at least $20 billion in fiscal 2027 free cash flow, he would exit. Otherwise, he believes investors are being offered substantial upside while paying a relatively modest price for the company’s future cash generation.

To this end, De Oliveira rates SNDK stock a Strong Buy. (To watch De Oliveira’s track record, click here)

That is also the conclusion reached by the analyst consensus, a rating based on 14 Buys and 2 Holds. Going by the $2,145 average price target, shares will appreciate by 19% in the months ahead. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: Intel vs. AMD: One AI Chip Stock Is Upgraded to Buy, the Other Will Underdeliver, Says Top Analyst
data.description:
For years, Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) have been locked in one of the semiconductor industry’s fiercest rivalries.  

Historically, Intel has been the far more dominant force, but the rivalry has entered a new phase, with AMD continuing to take market share from Intel even as the company has been mounting a comeback of its own.

The shift is unfolding as the AI boom reshapes demand for processors, accelerators, and data center infrastructure, creating significant opportunities for both chipmakers. For investors, that raises an obvious question: with both stocks having delivered enormous gains over the past year, which chip giant offers the better opportunity from here?

Learn more about TipRanks Premium

One top analyst has the answer to that question. Northland’s Gus Richard, an analyst ranked among the top 3% on Wall Street, sees meaningful developments on both sides of the rivalry, although his expectations for the two chipmakers diverge.

On the Intel side, Richard points to “material progress” in the company’s turnaround, as well as a shortage of server CPUs that could provide a near-term benefit. Additionally, he sees potential significance in Intel’s relationship with Elon Musk’s Terafab project, arguing that the partnership could provide the scale needed to strengthen Intel’s process technology footprint and support its foundry ambitions.

Richard also identifies geopolitics as a potential catalyst. In his view, it is not a question of whether China will reunify with Taiwan, but when. He believes China’s reunification with Taiwan could occur within the next 18 months, and argues that the conflict in Iran may have opened a window in which China could pursue a blockade of Taiwan. Taiwan’s 2028 presidential election represents another possible catalyst, in his view. Should these developments unfold, Richard believes Intel would be positioned to outperform.

That geopolitical backdrop could also enhance the strategic importance of the Terafab initiative. Richard points to Musk’s history of what he describes as “state symbiosis,” whereby the entrepreneur develops infrastructure that becomes strategically important to government, with SpaceX providing an example. Global capacity for wafers at 5nm and below is currently estimated at around 12 million 300mm wafers annually, while TSMC’s sub-5nm capacity is estimated at approximately 8 million. Across its lifetime, Musk’s Terafab is expected to reach annual capacity of 22.4 million advanced-logic wafers, although the entire facility is not expected to be completed until the late 2030s.

The first Terafab product is anticipated in 2028 or 2029. Building the initial stage is estimated to require $55 billion, while completing the entire project could cost as much as $120 billion. Richard puts that figure into perspective by estimating that TSMC will spend about $46 billion on sub-5nm capacity this year alone. He thinks that SpaceX, Tesla, and xAI are unlikely to provide enough demand to absorb the Terafab’s planned capacity during this decade. That raises the possibility, in his view, that the project’s extraordinary scale is ultimately designed to serve a strategic purpose beyond those companies, potentially substituting for some of TSMC’s manufacturing capacity in Taiwan. “Aligning with Musk’s Terafab boosts Intel’s turnaround efforts and validates its push into external foundry services,” the 5-star analyst summed up.

Against this backdrop, Richard has upgraded his INTC rating from Market Perform (i.e., Neutral) to Outperform (Buy). His $120 price target suggests shares will gain 19% in the months ahead. (To watch Richard’s track record, click here)

On the other side of the rivalry, for AMD, Richard offers a cautious take. He sees healthy demand across the company’s server CPU and GPU businesses, while embedded products are also performing well. Capacity, however, is limiting how much of that demand AMD can convert into growth. More importantly, Richard thinks expectations for 2027 have run too far ahead of what the industry can realistically deliver. His forecasts are well below consensus because he believes the current chip boom has bubble-like characteristics and that a portion of the data center projects being planned today will never translate into actual spending.

AMD is forecasting a sharp acceleration in its data center business, with growth expected to pick up during the second half of the year before more than doubling in 2027. That outlook would put data center revenue above $60 billion next year. Richard is taking a considerably more conservative position, modeling approximately $50 billion instead. A key concern is that some of the demand being reported may not represent genuine incremental consumption, with customers potentially placing overlapping or duplicate orders.

Richard also thinks there are practical limits to how quickly the industry can expand. Labor availability, power, memory, wafer supply, substrates, and access to capital could all constrain data center buildouts, even where customer demand remains strong. And with AMD serving a wide range of data center customers, Richard does not expect every customer to deliver on its stated spending plans.

As such, Richard rates AMD as Market Perform (i.e., Neutral) without having a fixed price target in mind.

In general, the rest of the Street takes the opposite stance. INTC stock only claims a Hold consensus rating, although its $116.31 average price target points toward 12-month returns of 15%. AMD, on the other hand, receives a Strong Buy consensus rating, while its $647.19 average target offers one-year upside of 32%. (See INTC stock forecast or AMD stock forecast)

data.title: Oracle Earnings Are Coming – Here’s Why Mizuho Sees 100% Upside for the AI Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is set to take center stage this week as the cloud computing giant prepares to report its fiscal first-quarter results after the close on Thursday, Sept. 10. The stock has struggled in 2026, largely because Oracle’s massive, debt-funded spending on AI infrastructure has weighed on free cash flow and contributed to credit downgrades.

Still, the shares have recovered sharply from their July lows. Despite remaining down 18% year to date, Oracle is now up 38% from its recent bottom, suggesting investor sentiment has started to improve.

Mizuho analyst Siti Panigrahi is also optimistic heading into the report, expecting Oracle to beat consensus estimates. The analyst sees OCI as the main source of upside, with around 1 gigawatt of new capacity expected to come online in the first quarter, compared with roughly 1.2 gigawatts added throughout fiscal 2026.

Consensus calls for $19.13 billion in revenue and $1.75 in adjusted EPS, but Panigrahi believes the more important issue will be how quickly Oracle converts its growing OCI backlog into revenue. IaaS revenue is expected to reach $7.19 billion, up 115% year over year, following 93% growth in the previous quarter.

Panigrahi expects the additional capacity to support strong OCI revenue conversion and reinforce confidence in Oracle’s fiscal 2027 revenue outlook. RPO (remaining performance obligations) should continue to grow as AI computing demand remains well ahead of supply, while non-AI OCI is benefiting from database modernization and Oracle’s multi-cloud relationships with Microsoft, Google and Amazon Web Services. The key, the analyst says, is whether Oracle can turn its backlog into revenue on schedule.

Panigrahi also sees an overlooked opportunity in Oracle’s applications and SaaS business, particularly through the rollout of Cerner with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. Consensus expects fiscal first-quarter SaaS revenue of $4.26 billion, up 11% year over year. With the NetSuite and small-business buying cycle largely behind Oracle and Cerner deployments picking up again, the analyst expects SaaS growth to accelerate in the coming quarters.

The VA has raised the ceiling on its Oracle Health contract to nearly $27 billion and resumed Cerner deployments following a three-year pause. Seven medical centers are expected to go live during Oracle’s first quarter, with another two slated for October. That number rises to 26 scheduled facilities in calendar 2027, compared with 13 in 2026.

Panigrahi highlights three areas investors should watch: how much new data center capacity Oracle adds and monetizes, particularly around projects such as Jupiter; any changes to its $90 billion-$95 billion fiscal 2027 gross CapEx outlook; and updates on the planned $20 billion equity-at-the-market offering and debt financing.

The analyst also believes Oracle’s use of customer prepayments and bring-your-own-hardware arrangements deserves more attention. These structures can reduce the strain on Oracle’s balance sheet while allowing the company to maintain its advantages in networking, clustering, RDMA and cloud operations. “We see a path for shares to re-rate as financing concerns fade, visibility builds toward FCF inflection, and Investor Day on Oct. 28 provides the next catalyst,” the analyst summed up.
